Appendix B Phase fix-up rotations in Hamming weight phasing

In this appendix, we derive the local phase corrections required when replacing controlled and directionally controlled towers of equiangular RzR_{z} rotations with controlled and directionally controlled HWP circuits, respectively. Recall that an RzR_{z} gate and phase gate (PP) are defined as

Rz​(θ)\displaystyle R_{z}(\theta) :=[e−iθ/200ei​θ/2],\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\theta/2}&0\\ 0&\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta/2}\end{bmatrix}, P⁡(θ)\displaystyle P(\theta) :=[100ei​θ],\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 0&\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}\end{bmatrix}, (33)

respectively.

Fix-up in controlled HWP.

A controlled RzR_{z} and a controlled phase rotation can be made equivalent by applying a phase fix-up as shown in Figure 34(a). In the context of this work, we are substituting a controlled tower of RzR_{z} rotations acting on L2L^{2} qubits with a controlled implementation of Hamming weight phasing. The controlled version of the original HWP circuit using GPGA, in which the payload rotation is a phase gate, synthesizes the controlled multi-target phase gate. This equivalence is shown in Figure 34(b). This leaves L2L^{2} applications of the phase fix-up gate, which accumulates to:

P⁡(−L2​θ2).P\bigg(-\frac{L^{2}\theta}{2}\bigg).

In other words, we need to correct by a local phase of −θ/2-\theta/2 for each rotation in the tower, and there are L2L^{2} of such rotations.

Fix-up in directionally controlled HWP.

The original circuit we are trying to substitute with a directionally controlled HWP is the following: a closed-controlled implementation of the (forward) Rz​(θ)R_{z}(\theta) tower and an open-controlled implementation of the (inverse) Rz​(−θ)R_{z}(-\theta) tower. That is, the angles between the two towers are equal in magnitude but opposite in sign. We can express the two controlled RzR_{z} towers in terms of two controlled phase rotation towers of opposite signs by leveraging the multi-target versions of the circuit equivalences Figure 34(a) and Figure 35. Substituting a controlled Rz​(θ)R_{z}(\theta) tower with a controlled P⁡(θ)P(\theta) tower contributes a phase fix-up gate of angle −L2θ/2-L^{2}\theta/2 acting on the |1⟩\lvert 1\rangle state of the control qubit, while the inverse case contributes a phase gate of angle L2​θ/2L^{2}\theta/2 acting on the |0⟩\lvert 0\rangle state of the control qubit. These two fix-up gates are equivalent to a single Rz​(−L2​θ)R_{z}(-L^{2}\theta) rotation on the control qubit, i.e. P⁡(−L2​θ)⋅X⋅P⁡(L2​θ)⋅X=Rz​(−L2​θ)P(-L^{2}\theta)\cdot X\cdot P(L^{2}\theta)\cdot X=R_{z}(-L^{2}\theta).

The directional implementation of HWP implements the forward and inverse towers of phase rotations by conjugating the circuit with open-controlled CNOT fanouts acting on the catalyst register. In addition, the payload rotation needs to be directionally controlled, applying P⁡(−2⌊log2⁡(L2)⌋+1​θ)P(-2^{\lfloor\log_{2}(L^{2})\rfloor+1}\theta) when the control qubit is |0⟩\lvert 0\rangle and P⁡(2⌊log2⁡(L2)⌋+1​θ)P(2^{\lfloor\log_{2}(L^{2})\rfloor+1}\theta) when the control qubit is |1⟩\lvert 1\rangle. These two controlled payload rotations can be simplified to two uncontrolled phase rotations:

where we replace two controlled phase gates with an uncontrolled payload phase gate and a local phase correction of angle −2⌊log2⁡(L2)⌋+1​θ-2^{\lfloor\log_{2}(L^{2})\rfloor+1}\theta.

The phase corrections therefore combine into a single local rotation

Rz​(−L2​θ+2⌊log2⁡(L2)⌋+1​θ),R_{z}\left(-L^{2}\theta+2^{\lfloor\log_{2}(L^{2})\rfloor+1}\theta\right),

up to an overall global phase.

Accumulated phase corrections.

Within a directionally controlled Trotter step, the local phase corrections introduced by successive directionally controlled HWP calls all act on the same QPE control qubit and therefore commute. Consequently, they may be combined into a single RzR_{z} rotation on each of the k−1k-1 directionally controlled phase qubits.

Each plaquette HWP contributes a phase correction of

Rz​(−L2​θplaq+2⌊log2⁡(L2)⌋+1​θplaq),R_{z}(-L^{2}\theta_{\mathrm{plaq}}+2^{\lfloor\log_{2}(L^{2})\rfloor+1}\theta_{\mathrm{plaq}}),

while each interaction HWP contributes

Rz​(−L2​θint+2⌊log2⁡(L2)⌋+1​θint),R_{z}(-L^{2}\theta_{\mathrm{int}}+2^{\lfloor\log_{2}(L^{2})\rfloor+1}\theta_{\mathrm{int}}),

where θplaq\theta_{\mathrm{plaq}} and θint\theta_{\mathrm{int}} are the payload rotation angles for the plaquette and interaction HWP circuits, respectively.

The accumulated correction on the (j+1)(j+1)-th QPE phase qubit is therefore

Rz​(2j​r​[−L2​(θplaq+θint)+2⌊log2⁡(L2)⌋+1​(θplaq+θint)]),j∈[0,k−2],R_{z}\bigg(2^{j}r\left[-L^{2}\left(\theta_{\mathrm{plaq}}+\theta_{\mathrm{int}}\right)+2^{\lfloor\log_{2}(L^{2})\rfloor+1}\left(\theta_{\mathrm{plaq}}+\theta_{\mathrm{int}}\right)\right]\bigg),\qquad j\in[0,k-2],

where rr is the number of Trotter steps. The accumulated corrections over the k−1k-1 directionally controlled phase qubits therefore form a generalized phase gradient. Since this phase gradient is uncontrolled, it can be synthesized directly using GPGA using k−1k-1 Toffoli gates and a single phase rotation, without requiring any additional phase-fixup correction.

Appendix C Error budgeting details

We use an effective-Hamiltonian analysis to relate the unitary error, which naturally characterizes the circuit approximation, to the resulting error in the estimated energy. Any unitary operator can be written in the form U⁡(s)=ei​H​sU(s)=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}Hs} for some Hermitian operator HH. Accordingly, any approximate unitary U~​(s)\tilde{U}(s) can be expressed as ei​Heff​s\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}H_{\text{eff}}s} for some effective Hamiltonian HeffH_{\text{eff}} that will depend on ss. This allows us to bound the unitary error in terms of the resulting eigenenergy deviations [13, 55]:

‖U⁡(s)−U~​(s)‖=‖ei​H​s−ei​Heff​s‖≥|ei​E(k)​s−ei​Eeff(k)​s|=2​sin⁡(|E(k)−Eeff(k)|​s2),\displaystyle\|U(s)-\tilde{U}(s)\|=\|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}Hs}-\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}H_{\text{eff}}s}\|\geq\left|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}E^{(k)}s}-\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}E^{(k)}_{\text{eff}}s}\right|=2\sin\left(\frac{|E^{(k)}-E^{(k)}_{\text{eff}}|s}{2}\right), (34)

for all kk-th eigenvalues of HH and HeffH_{\text{eff}}. Equivalently:

|E(k)−Eeff(k)|≤2s​arcsin⁡(‖U​(s)−U~​(s)‖2)≤ϵeff.\displaystyle\mathinner{\!\left\lvert E^{(k)}-E^{(k)}_{\text{eff}}\right\rvert}\leq\frac{2}{s}\arcsin\left(\frac{\|U(s)-\tilde{U}(s)\|}{2}\right)\leq\epsilon_{\text{eff}}. (35)

We use the right hand inequality of Eq. 35 to relate the allowable unitary error from the energy budget:

‖VQPE​(U~)−V~QPE​(U~)‖≤2​sin⁡(ϵcat​τ2),\|V_{\text{QPE}(\tilde{U})}-\tilde{V}_{\text{QPE}(\tilde{U})}\|\leq 2\sin\left(\frac{\epsilon_{\text{cat}}\tau}{2}\right), (36)
‖U⁡(τ)−(Uτ/r)r‖+‖(Uτ/r)r−(U~τ/r)r‖≤2​sin⁡(ϵU​τ2).\|U(\tau)-(U_{\tau/r})^{r}\|+\|(U_{\tau/r})^{r}-(\tilde{U}_{\tau/r})^{r}\|\leq 2\sin\left(\frac{\epsilon_{U}\tau}{2}\right). (37)

To simplify the optimization, we perform a first-order approximation of the arcsin\arcsin function which introduces negligible error in the regime of interest1515 15 Note that if we were to include error budget for the QFT and window state preparation in QPE implementation error, one could replace ϵcat\epsilon_{\text{cat}} by ϵV\epsilon_{V} and use a similar approximation ϵV≈ϵcat+ϵQFT+ϵwindow\epsilon_{V}\approx\epsilon_{\text{cat}}+\epsilon_{\text{QFT}}+\epsilon_{\text{window}}.:

ϵU\displaystyle\epsilon_{U} ≥2τ​arcsin⁡(‖U⁡(τ)−(Uτ/r)r‖+‖(Uτ/r)r−(U~τ/r)r‖2)\displaystyle\geq\frac{2}{\tau}\arcsin\left(\frac{\|U(\tau)-(U_{\tau/r})^{r}\|+\|(U_{\tau/r})^{r}-(\tilde{U}_{\tau/r})^{r}\|}{2}\right) (38a)
≈2τ​(arcsin⁡(‖U⁡(τ)−(Uτ/r)r‖2)+arcsin⁡(‖(Uτ/r)r−(U~τ/r)r‖2))\displaystyle\approx\frac{2}{\tau}\left(\arcsin\left(\frac{\|U(\tau)-(U_{\tau/r})^{r}\|}{2}\right)+\arcsin\left(\frac{\|(U_{\tau/r})^{r}-(\tilde{U}_{\tau/r})^{r}\|}{2}\right)\right) (38b)
=ϵST+ϵrot.\displaystyle=\epsilon_{\text{ST}}+\epsilon_{\text{rot}}. (38c)

This allows for a linear attribution of the energy error to each source:

ϵ\displaystyle\epsilon ≥ϵQPE+ϵST+ϵrot+ϵcat\displaystyle\geq\epsilon_{\text{QPE}}+\epsilon_{\text{ST}}+\epsilon_{\text{rot}}+\epsilon_{\text{cat}} (39a)
=ϵ⁡[δQPE+(1−δQPE)​(δST+(1−δST)​(δrot+(1−δrot)))]\displaystyle=\epsilon\Big[\delta_{\text{QPE}}+(1-\delta_{\text{QPE}})\Big(\delta_{\text{ST}}+(1-\delta_{\text{ST}})\big(\delta_{\text{rot}}+(1-\delta_{\text{rot}})\big)\Big)\Big] (39b)
=δQPE​ϵ+(1−δQPE)​δST​ϵ+(1−δQPE)​(1−δST)​δrot​ϵ+(1−δQPE)​(1−δST)​(1−δrot)​ϵ.\displaystyle=\delta_{\text{QPE}}\epsilon+(1-\delta_{\text{QPE}})\delta_{\text{ST}}\epsilon+(1-\delta_{\text{QPE}})(1-\delta_{\text{ST}})\delta_{\text{rot}}\epsilon+(1-\delta_{\text{QPE}})(1-\delta_{\text{ST}})(1-\delta_{\text{rot}})\epsilon. (39c)

By construction, all error allocation parameters δ\delta lie in the interval (0,1)(0,1) which ensures the equality in Eq. 39a. The optimization is therefore performed over the parameters {δQPE,δST,δrot,τ}\{\delta_{\text{QPE}},\delta_{\text{ST}},\delta_{\text{rot}},\tau\} using SciPy’s basin-hopping algorithm with L-BFGS-B as the local minimizer [97].

We set the search bounds of the evolution time in the optimization to [τmin,τmax][\tau_{\min},\tau_{\max}]. A conservative choice for τmax\tau_{\max} is 2​π/‖HFH‖12\pi/\|H_{\text{FH}}\|_{1} to avoid aliasing [75, 9]1616 16 Aliasing occurs when eigenphases are not properly constrained to the interval [0,2​π)[0,2\pi), causing them to “wrap around” in phase space.. However, this bound is overly restrictive for Trotter-based approaches which, unlike qubitization, can exploit aliasing in ground-state energy estimation by increasing the evolution time. Increasing the evolution time reduces QPE error but increases Trotter error, leading to an optimal trade-off point that often exceeds 2​π/‖HFH‖12\pi/\|H_{\text{FH}}\|_{1}. Practically, as classical methods already provide ground-state energy estimates to some coarse precision, the quantum algorithm is used only to resolve the remaining bits. Using well-established classical techniques, Ref. [57] provides benchmark zero-temperature estimates from AFQMC, DMRG, fixed-node QMC, and DMET that already form a relatively narrow but still non-negligible band in the challenging regime U/t=8U/t=8, and average electron density per site of 0.8750.875: DMRG gave E/Lx​Ly​t≈−0.759​(4)E/L_{x}L_{y}t\approx-0.759(4), and fixed-node VMC gave −0.749​(2)-0.749(2). Thus, at this benchmark point, the spread is approximately 0.02​t0.02t per site. To remain conservative, we take the accuracy achievable with these established classical methods, 1717 17 We note that classical accuracy has improved significantly in recent years through advances such as VAFQMC, neural quantum states, and tensor-backflow methods [92, 60, 81, 61, 98]; however, we retain the conservative estimate here. to be about 5%​t5\%\,t per site. We set the optimizer’s upper bound on the evolution time based on this classical accuracy, i.e. τmax=2​π/(0.05​t​Lx​Ly)\tau_{\max}=2\pi/(0.05tL_{x}L_{y}). While the optimal time often exceeds 2​π/‖HFH‖12\pi/\|H_{\text{FH}}\|_{1}, it remains well within the τmax\tau_{\max} limit imposed by classical precision.

C.1 Suzuki-Trotter error methodology

The goal of this section is to generalize the analytic commutator bounds of Ref. [20] to arbitrary second-order Suzuki product formulas, allowing different Hamiltonian decompositions, Trotter orderings, lattice geometries, and hopping ranges. Rather than evaluating commutator norms on exponentially large Hilbert-space operators, our objective is to estimate the Trotter error using only operations acting on matrices whose dimension scales with the number of fermionic modes. This provides an automated procedure for evaluating commutator bounds for a broad class of Hubbard Hamiltonians.

To this end, we represent the one- and two-body components of the Hubbard Hamiltonian by

T⁡(Λ)\displaystyle T(\Lambda) =∑j​k∑σ=↑,↓Λj​k​cj​σ†​ck​σ,\displaystyle=\sum_{jk}\sum_{\sigma=\uparrow,\downarrow}\Lambda_{jk}c^{\dagger}_{j\sigma}c_{k\sigma}, (40)
U⁡(v)\displaystyle U(v) =∑kvk​Zk↑​Zk↓,\displaystyle=\sum_{k}v_{k}Z_{k\uparrow}Z_{k\downarrow}, (41)

where Zk​σ=1−2​ck​σ†​ck​σZ_{k\sigma}=1-2c^{\dagger}_{k\sigma}c_{k\sigma}, Λ\Lambda is the hopping matrix, and vv specifies the onsite interaction strengths.

Consider a second-order Suzuki product formula composed of Hamiltonians H1,H2,…,HLH_{1},H_{2},\ldots,H_{L} each of which is represented by a pair (Λi,vi)(\Lambda_{i},v_{i}). The corresponding product formula is

S2(s)=ei​H1​s/2ei​H2​s/2⋯ei​HL−1​s/2ei​HL​sei​HL−1​s/2⋯ei​H2​s/2ei​H1​s/2S_{2}(s)=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}H_{1}s/2}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}H_{2}s/2}\cdots\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}H_{L-1}s/2}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}H_{L}s}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}H_{L-1}s/2}\cdots\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}H_{2}s/2}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}H_{1}s/2} (42)

whose error is bounded by the telescopic commutator expansion

‖S2​(s)−ei​∑kHk​s‖≤|s|3​∑k=1L(112​‖[[ℒk,Hk],ℒk]‖+124​‖[[ℒk,Hk],Hk]‖),\left\|\vphantom{\sum}S_{2}(s)-\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\sum_{k}H_{k}s}\right\|\leq\mathinner{\!\left\lvert s\right\rvert}^{3}\sum_{k=1}^{L}\left(\frac{1}{12}\left\|\left[\left[\vphantom{\sum}\mathcal{L}_{k},H_{k}\right],\mathcal{L}_{k}\vphantom{\sum_{k}}\right]\right\|+\frac{1}{24}\left\|\left[\left[\vphantom{\sum}\mathcal{L}_{k},H_{k}\right],H_{k}\vphantom{\sum_{k}}\right]\right\|\right)\,, (43)

where

ℒk=∑m>kHm\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{k}=\sum_{m>k}H_{m} (44)

is the accumulated Hamiltonian following HkH_{k} in the Suzuki ordering.

The problem therefore reduces to estimating the two classes of nested commutators appearing in Eq. 43 using only the matrices Λi\Lambda_{i} and vectors viv_{i}. To accomplish this, we introduce a generic double commutator that encompasses every contribution to the telescopic bound and derive matrix-based expressions and norm bounds for each of its constituent terms.

The two nested commutators appearing in Eq. 43 differ only in the choice of their three Hamiltonian arguments. Since each Hamiltonian is specified by a matrix-vector pair (Λ,v)(\Lambda,v), it is sufficient to derive a bound for the generic operator

G⁡(A,B,C,a,b,c)≔[[T⁡(A)+U⁡(a),T⁡(B)+U⁡(b)],T⁡(C)+U⁡(c)]G(A,B,C,a,b,c)\coloneqq\left[\vphantom{\sum_{k}}\left[\vphantom{\sum}T(A)+U(a),\;T(B)+U(b)\right],\;T(C)+U(c)\right] (45)

with the matrices A,B,CA,B,C and vectors a,b,ca,b,c.

Lemma 1.

Let AA, BB and CC be hopping matrices and let aa, bb and cc be interaction vectors. Then G⁡(A,B,C,a,b,c)G(A,B,C,a,b,c) as defined in Eq. 45 is norm bounded by

‖G⁡(A,B,C,a,b,c)‖≤2​‖Tσ​([[A,B],C]+4​{A,Db​Dc}−4​{B,Da​Dc})‖+8​‖Tσ​(Db​A​Dc+Dc​A​Db−Da​B​Dc−Dc​B​Da)‖+4​∑j‖[bj​Qj​σ​(A)−aj​Qj​σ​(B),Tσ​(C)]+cj​Qj​σ​([A,B])‖+8∑j∥Qj​σ(C)∥∥bjQj​σ(A)−ajQj​σ(B)∥.\begin{multlined}\|G(A,B,C,a,b,c)\|\leq 2\left\|T_{\sigma}\!\left([[A,B],C]+4\{A,D_{b}D_{c}\}-4\{B,D_{a}D_{c}\}\right)\right\|+\\ 8\left\|T_{\sigma}\!\left(D_{b}AD_{c}+D_{c}AD_{b}-D_{a}BD_{c}-D_{c}BD_{a}\right)\right\|+4\sum_{j}\left\|\left[b_{j}Q_{j\sigma}(A)-a_{j}Q_{j\sigma}(B),T_{\sigma}(C)\right]+c_{j}Q_{j\sigma}([A,B])\right\|\\ +8\sum_{j}\|Q_{j\sigma}(C)\|\,\|b_{j}Q_{j\sigma}(A)-a_{j}Q_{j\sigma}(B)\|.\end{multlined}

Here DxD_{x} denotes the diagonal matrix with entries (Dx)j​k=xj​δj​k(D_{x})_{jk}=x_{j}\delta_{jk}, {⋅,⋅}\{\cdot,\cdot\} denotes the matrix anticommutator, and

Qj​σ​(A)≔∑k(Aj​k​cj​σ†​ck​σ−Ak​j​ck​σ†​cj​σ)Q_{j\sigma}(A)\coloneqq\sum_{k}\left(A_{jk}c^{\dagger}_{j\sigma}c_{k\sigma}-A_{kj}c^{\dagger}_{k\sigma}c_{j\sigma}\right)

is the star operator associated with the jjth site.

The significance of Lemma 1 is that every quantity on the right-hand side can be evaluated using only matrices of dimension equal to the number of fermionic modes. In particular, the norm of Tσ​(A)T_{\sigma}(A) is determined by the spectrum of AA, while the norm of Qj​σ​(A)Q_{j\sigma}(A) is determined by the spectrum of the matrix Dj​A−A​DjD_{j}A-AD_{j}. Consequently, the many-body commutator bound is reduced to a sequence of polynomial-cost matrix operations.

For the kk’th contribution to the telescopic bound, the arguments (B,b)(B,b) are identified with the Hamiltonian parameters (Λk,vk)(\Lambda_{k},v_{k}), while (A,a)(A,a) correspond to the accumulated Hamiltonian parameters

(A,a)=(∑m>kΛm,∑m>kvm).(A,a)=\left(\sum_{m>k}\Lambda_{m},\sum_{m>k}v_{m}\right). (46)

The two nested commutators in Eq. 43 are then obtained by choosing (C,c)=(A,a)(C,c)=(A,a) for [[ℒk,Hk],ℒk][[\mathcal{L}_{k},H_{k}],\mathcal{L}_{k}] and (C,c)=(B,b)(C,c)=(B,b) for [[ℒk,Hk],Hk][[\mathcal{L}_{k},H_{k}],H_{k}]. Applying Lemma 1 therefore yields every contribution required to evaluate the second-order Suzuki error bound. The remainder of this appendix is a proof of the technical result.

Proof.

We begin by decomposing GG into simpler nested commutators according to the one- and two-body components of the Hamiltonians. Expanding the nested commutator using linearity isolates the distinct combinations of one- and two-body Hamiltonians that must be bounded. Since [U⁡(a),U⁡(b)]=0[U(a),U(b)]=0, only six terms remain,

G⁡(A,B,C,a,b,c)=[[T⁡(A),T⁡(B)],T⁡(C)]+[[T⁡(A),U⁡(b)],T⁡(C)]−[[T⁡(B),U⁡(a)],T⁡(C)]+[[T⁡(A),T⁡(B)],U⁡(c)]+[[T⁡(A),U⁡(b)],U⁡(c)]−[[T⁡(B),U⁡(a)],U⁡(c)].\begin{multlined}G(A,B,C,a,b,c)=\left[\left[T(A),T(B)\right],T(C)\right]+\left[\left[T(A),U(b)\right],T(C)\right]-\left[\left[T(B),U(a)\right],T(C)\right]\\ +\left[\left[T(A),T(B)\right],U(c)\right]+\left[\left[T(A),U(b)\right],U(c)\right]-\left[\left[T(B),U(a)\right],U(c)\right].\end{multlined} (47)

The first term is simply

[[T⁡(A),T⁡(B)],T⁡(C)]=T⁡([[A,B],C]),\left[\left[T(A),T(B)\right],T(C)\right]=T([[A,B],C]), (48)

using the identity [T⁡(A),T⁡(B)]=T⁡([A,B])[T(A),T(B)]=T([A,B]).

Using the canonical anticommutation relations, the number operator nk​σ≔ck​σ†​ck​σn_{k\sigma}\coloneqq c^{\dagger}_{k\sigma}c_{k\sigma} satisfies

[nk​σ,cj​σ†​cℓ​σ]=(δk​j−δk​ℓ)​cj​σ†​cℓ​σ.[n_{k\sigma},c^{\dagger}_{j\sigma}c_{\ell\sigma}]=(\delta_{kj}-\delta_{k\ell})c^{\dagger}_{j\sigma}c_{\ell\sigma}. (49)

Equivalently, [nk​σ,ck​σ†​cj​σ]=ck​σ†​cj​σ[n_{k\sigma},c^{\dagger}_{k\sigma}c_{j\sigma}]=c^{\dagger}_{k\sigma}c_{j\sigma} and [nk​σ,cj​σ†​ck​σ]=−cj​σ†​ck​σ[n_{k\sigma},c^{\dagger}_{j\sigma}c_{k\sigma}]=-c^{\dagger}_{j\sigma}c_{k\sigma}. Since Zk​σ=1−2​nk​σZ_{k\sigma}=1-2n_{k\sigma}, Eq. 49 gives

[T⁡(A),U⁡(b)]\displaystyle[T(A),U(b)] =2​∑j​k,σAj​k​(bj​Zj​σ¯−bk​Zk​σ¯)​cj​σ†​ck​σ\displaystyle=2\sum_{jk,\sigma}A_{jk}\left(b_{j}Z_{j\bar{\sigma}}-b_{k}Z_{k\bar{\sigma}}\right)c^{\dagger}_{j\sigma}c_{k\sigma} (50a)
=2​∑j,σbj​Zj​σ¯​Qj​σ​(A).\displaystyle=2\sum_{j,\sigma}b_{j}Z_{j\bar{\sigma}}Q_{j\sigma}(A). (50b)

Hence

[[T⁡(A),T⁡(B)],U⁡(c)]\displaystyle[[T(A),T(B)],U(c)] =2​∑j,σcj​Zj​σ¯​Qj​σ​([A,B]),\displaystyle=2\sum_{j,\sigma}c_{j}Z_{j\bar{\sigma}}Q_{j\sigma}([A,B]), (51)
[[T⁡(A),U⁡(b)],T⁡(C)]\displaystyle[[T(A),U(b)],T(C)] =2​∑j,σbj​(Zj​σ¯​[Qj​σ​(A),Tσ​(C)]−2​Qj​σ​(A)​Qj​σ¯​(C)).\displaystyle=2\sum_{j,\sigma}b_{j}\left(Z_{j\bar{\sigma}}\left[Q_{j\sigma}(A),T_{\sigma}(C)\right]-2Q_{j\sigma}(A)Q_{j\bar{\sigma}}(C)\right). (52)

Subtracting the corresponding expression with (A,b)↔(B,a)(A,b)\leftrightarrow(B,a) gives

,T(C)]−[[T(B),U(a)],T(C)]=2∑j,σZj​σ¯[bjQj​σ(A)−ajQj​σ(B),Tσ(C)]−4∑j,σ(bjQj​σ(A)−ajQj​σ(B))Qj​σ¯(C).\begin{multlined},T(C)]-[[T(B),U(a)],T(C)]=2\sum_{j,\sigma}Z_{j\bar{\sigma}}\left[b_{j}Q_{j\sigma}(A)-a_{j}Q_{j\sigma}(B),T_{\sigma}(C)\right]\\ -4\sum_{j,\sigma}\left(b_{j}Q_{j\sigma}(A)-a_{j}Q_{j\sigma}(B)\right)Q_{j\bar{\sigma}}(C).\end{multlined} (53)

Finally, letting DxD_{x} denote the diagonal matrix with entries (Dx)j​k=xj​δj​k(D_{x})_{jk}=x_{j}\delta_{jk}, there exists a unitary VV such that

,U(c)]=4T({A,DbDc})−4V†T(DbADc+DcADb)V,\begin{multlined},U(c)]=4T\!\left(\{A,D_{b}D_{c}\}\right)-4V^{\dagger}T\!\left(D_{b}AD_{c}+D_{c}AD_{b}\right)V,\end{multlined} (54)

and hence

[[T⁡(A),U⁡(b)],U⁡(c)]−[[T⁡(B),U⁡(a)],U⁡(c)]\displaystyle[[T(A),U(b)],U(c)]-[[T(B),U(a)],U(c)]

G⁡(A,B,C,a,b,c)=∑σTσ​([[A,B],C]+4​{A,Db​Dc}−4​{B,Da​Dc})−4∑σV†Tσ(DbADc+DcADb−DaBDc−DcBDa)V+2∑j,σZj​σ¯([bjQj​σ(A)−ajQj​σ(B),Tσ(C)]+cjQj​σ([A,B]))−4∑j,σ(bjQj​σ(A)−ajQj​σ(B))Qj​σ¯(C).\begin{multlined}G(A,B,C,a,b,c)=\sum_{\sigma}T_{\sigma}\!\left([[A,B],C]+4\{A,D_{b}D_{c}\}-4\{B,D_{a}D_{c}\}\right)\\ -4\sum_{\sigma}V^{\dagger}T_{\sigma}\!\left(D_{b}AD_{c}+D_{c}AD_{b}-D_{a}BD_{c}-D_{c}BD_{a}\right)V\\ +2\sum_{j,\sigma}Z_{j\bar{\sigma}}\left(\left[b_{j}Q_{j\sigma}(A)-a_{j}Q_{j\sigma}(B),T_{\sigma}(C)\right]+c_{j}Q_{j\sigma}([A,B])\right)\\ -4\sum_{j,\sigma}\left(b_{j}Q_{j\sigma}(A)-a_{j}Q_{j\sigma}(B)\right)Q_{j\bar{\sigma}}(C).\end{multlined} (56)

Appendix D Data for quantum resource estimates

This section includes additional data on the reported quantum resource estimates for reproducibility.

Details of the baseline circuit recorded for comparison in the results are described in Table 5. For both implementations, we first consider a single batch of rotations for Hamming-weight phasing; the impact of varying the number of batches is investigated later in this section.

We verified the baseline circuit construction by reproducing the Toffoli count derived in Ref. [52]. We implemented the equations from Kan et al. assuming a single batch of rotations for Hamming weight phasing and multiplying the cost per query by the number of queries from the error budget optimization. The two sets of counts, as shown in Figure 37, agree perfectly across all lattice sizes. We then constructed the improved circuit by replacing baseline subroutines with their active volume optimized counterparts, updating circuit parameters such as rotation synthesis errors, and implementing appropriate controlled query structures based on the choice of QPE.

To produce our resource estimates we optimize the error parameters within the error budget constraint, the data for batch sizes β=1,2\beta=1,2 are reported in Table 6.

Appendix E Hardware model for runtime estimates

The active volume architecture is well-suited for photonic quantum computing. It makes use of a logarithmic number of non-local swap operations per qubit to substantially reduce idle times. In a photonic quantum computer, these non-local operations can be facilitated by optical switching and fiber-delay lines, although they may also be implemented in other architectures. For this work, we adopt the photonic hardware parameters summarized in Table 7, following Refs. [15, 62, 18, 42].

Our resource estimates use the block scheduler [41] to assign each lattice-surgery operation to a logical cycle, rather than estimating runtime from operation counts alone. The resulting schedule requires ℓ\ell logical cycles. Given a machine containing ntn_{t} logical qubits, including both memory and workspace, we model the logical failure probability per qubit per logical cycle as

pL(d)=10−αd/2.p_{\mathrm{L}}(d)=10^{-\alpha d/2}. (57)

Assuming independent fault locations, we choose the smallest permitted code distance dd satisfying

1−(1−pL​(d))nt​ℓ≤pf,1-\left(1-p_{\mathrm{L}}(d)\right)^{n_{t}\ell}\leq p_{f}, (58)

where pfp_{f} is the allocated probability of hardware-induced failure over the complete computation.

A logical cycle comprises dd code cycles, so its duration and the resulting runtime are

tlc=d​tcc,trun=ℓ​d​tcc.t_{\mathrm{lc}}=d\,t_{\mathrm{cc}},\qquad t_{\mathrm{run}}=\ell d\,t_{\mathrm{cc}}. (59)

The reaction time trt_{\mathrm{r}} is distinct from the code-cycle time tcct_{\mathrm{cc}}. It characterizes the latency of measurement-dependent classical processing and feed-forward, and therefore constrains the number of sequential reaction layers that can be completed within a logical cycle.

To further reduce runtime, we used an improved version of the scheduler introduced in [42], which will be described in more detail in an upcoming manuscript [19]. Unlike the original approach, which assembles the schedule from separate circuit segments, this scheduler is fast enough to process entire circuits. This is achieved by limiting the size of the directed acyclic graph (DAG) used to store the execution order of operations. While previous work has applied simpler DAG-based approaches to this problem [82, 89], we use a sliding-window DAG [43], yielding a substantial reduction in compilation time compared with the implementation described in [41]. Once the DAG exceeds a specified size (500500 operations in this case) the oldest operations are removed and scheduled.
